newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Lights to be switched back on at Marcos mausoleum.
newsitem.headline: Lights to be switched back on at Marcos mausoleum.

text.p: Power was expected to be restored on Wednesday to the mausoleum of late president Ferdinand Marcos, whose preserved corpse had been left in the dark in a dispute over unpaid electricity bills, officials said.
A second-hand generator was to be brought in to restart the lighting and air-conditioning systems of the mausoleum, where the former president lies in a glass coffin.

The huge tomb in Marcos' hometown in the northern Philippines was plunged into darkness on Monday when a local electric cooperative cut off its power over the family's refusal to settle electric bills totalling 5.6 million pesos ($214,500).
"I just talked to the former first lady and I told her that I will be bringing a generator today to give power to the mausoleum and the water pump," Batac Mayor Jesus Nalupta told Reuters.
"The generator will come any time today, so power will be restored today," he said.
"It is an old one," he said of the generator.

Nalupta said he had also written to the Ilocos Norte Electric Cooperative promising to pay part of the unpaid bills and asking for "re-connection of the power in deferral and respect to the former president."
Marcos's widow, Imelda, accused on Tuesday the government of dishonoring her husband.
"It's shocking," Marcos, almost in tears, told Reuters in Manila. "Is this the policy of government? It is so macabre ... This is not done to human beings, least of all to the dead."

Marcos, now a congresswoman who lives in a posh high-rise condominium in Manila's Makati financial centre, said she could not pay the bills because the government had seized all of the family's property.
The government accuses the family of stealing up to $5 billion from the economy during their 20-year rule and has sequestered their assets pending a court ruling on their ownership.
The former president was ousted in a 1986 "people power" revolt and died in exile in Hawaii three years later.
President Fidel Ramos, now visiting India, allowed the remains to be brought to Batac in 1993 but refused to allow his burial in Manila, fearing it would provoke violence.

Since then, the corpse has lain in an elevated glass coffin in the air-conditioned mausoleum in the family backyard. Embalmers injected it with chemicals which they said would preserve it for 10 years.
Up until Monday, the wax-like cadaver had been bathed in soft lights 24 hours a day while music by Mozart and other classical masters played in the background.
A sign hanging outside the mausoleum read, "BROWNOUT".

Ramos said in an interview with Reuters in New Delhi on Tuesday that the Marcos family could bury his corpse in Manila, but not in the Heroes Cemetery, where soldiers lie and where the family says his body deserves to buried.
"There are so many cemeteries in Manila that will take him. But we have one cemetery for the heroes which requires presidential approval," Ramos said.
There was no immediate reaction from the Marcos family to Ramos's suggestion.
Reuters journalists and a few curious visitors visited the dark mausoleum on Tuesday and, using flashlights, peered at Marcos's face.
"He's perspiring," visitor Visy Singson said on seeing the corpse.
Embalmer Frank Malabed said earlier it was normal for a preserved body kept in an air-conditioned room to develop moisture after power had been shut off.
